The passage is about Desiderius Erasmus, a Dutch Renaissance humanist and theologian. The text discusses his work, particularly his "Method of True Theology" and his paraphrases of the New Testament. It also mentions his criticisms of the doctrines and morals of the Reformers, and his treatment of each individual book of the scriptures as a literary unit in his paraphrases.

Regarding the Genesis account, recent studies question the analysis of E and J as strictly separate. Coats argues that Abraham's obedience to God's command necessitates praise and blessing, which he only receives in the second angelic speech. This has suggested to many that the author responsible for the interpolation of the second angelic appearance has left his mark also on the original account (v. 1–13, 19).

In terms of Erasmus' paraphrases, he gives paraphrases of the speech of Christ in the persona of Christ in the Gospels, and for each Epistle uses the voice of the Apostle, not Erasmus or a neutral third person as is conventional. Unlike traditional medieval exegesis, which for some authors treated the whole scriptures as a single unified document of propositions which, because they had the same divine author, could be mixed and matched as necessary, Erasmus treated each individual book as the literary unit that limited intertextual combination.

The passage also mentions Erasmus' criticisms of the doctrines and morals of the Reformers, comparing them unfavorably to the Catholic Church. He complains that the Reformers retain abuses in prayers, fasts, and Masses, and that they have not reclaimed people from sin as effectively as the Gospel promises. He also criticizes the Reformers' doctrines, likening them to the public Scholastic disputations he had previously criticized.
